actionThatDiffers: You answer the blocking prompt (approve a tool call, pick an option) from wherever you are instead of first switching to the pane to discover the question; and you triage which blocked session to answer first by what it wants.
why: The question text is literally on screen in the session's own pane; a six-line tmux capture-pane loop tailing each pane yields an adequate approximation of what every blocked session is asking, so this is reachable-with-manual-work, not hidden. Impact is real because the differing action is concrete and recurs many times a day: cheap approvals get handled immediately, expensive design questions get deferred, and no context switch is spent just to learn the question.

actionThatDiffers: You land in the right session in one keystroke instead of cycling tabs or panes to identify which of 12 is the one you just read about.
why: Kind is action: this is something the user DOES. Doing it today is Cmd+1..9, a tmux select-window, or clicking the tab, all one move in a place the user already knows, so access sits in the one-click band. The delta is a few seconds of tab-hunting per jump, which is convenience rather than loss prevention, so impact stays in the minor-action band even though the jump happens often.

actionThatDiffers: You push, PR, or intentionally delete a branch a finished session left sitting with unpushed commits, instead of discovering it weeks later or redoing the work on a fresh branch.
why: Every input is a known command (git status, git branch -vv, gh pr list --author @me), but the answer needs those run per repository and then correlated against which sessions actually ended, which is several places and manual work rather than one look. A loop over repo dirs gives an adequate approximation, so it caps in the reachable band. Impact is high because the differing action prevents concrete loss: abandoned work with real commits in it, or duplicated effort.

actionThatDiffers: On return you go straight to the one or two sessions that went wrong or finished, instead of reading back through 8 panes of scrollback to work out which ones need you.
why: capture-pane -S can dump scrollback, so the raw material is reachable, but the digest itself is a summary across every session AND across the whole away window, which is exactly the correlate-across-sessions-and-time work a normal user will not do reliably. Nothing anywhere computes the summary, so its value rests on the summarizer picking the right events. The differing action is real and recurring (targeted re-entry instead of a 10-minute read) but it saves minutes, not lost work.

actionThatDiffers: You notice a hosted or cowork run has finished or is blocked and respond to it, instead of it sitting unattended because it is not in any terminal you have open.
why: Hosted and cowork sessions live in a web UI the user can open in one click, so each is a known place to look; the cost is that it is a second surface in a different app from the terminals, which is tedium plus one more tab, not inaccessibility. The differing action is genuine but bounded: for a user whose 3-12 sessions are mostly local terminals this covers a minority of the fleet, so it is a mild-to-moderate convenience rather than loss prevention. Briefing does not cover cowork, so confidence is low.

actionThatDiffers: none - the item's own stated outcome is "no decision attached"; knowing a CLI is on 1.2.3 does not change what the user does next.
why: claude --version, codex --version and friends are one command each in a place the user already knows, so access is squarely in the one-command band. No concrete different action can be named, so impact stays in the interesting-but-inert band; version drift only matters when something has already broken, at which point the user runs the version command anyway. Partial shipped state gets the same scrutiny: being displayed does not make it valuable.

actionThatDiffers: You act on a session running on a remote dev box or second machine (answer its prompt, stop it) without SSHing in to check; for teammates, nothing you can act on today at all.
why: The tmux loop only works on the machine you are sitting at. Other machines require SSH plus repeating the sweep per host, and a teammate's sessions have no local data source whatsoever, so by hand this is at the edge of unobtainable. Impact is held down by the lens: the normal user here runs 3-12 sessions on one laptop, so the fleet view changes their behaviour only occasionally, when a remote box is in play. That is a real but infrequent decision, not a recurring one.

actionThatDiffers: You resume or close a session you had forgotten was open, reclaiming the pane and catching whatever it was mid-way through, instead of leaving it parked indefinitely.
why: This is an arithmetic composite: last-activity timestamp compared against a 2-hour threshold. The input is individually visible (the pane shows when it last printed; session file mtimes and ps give the same thing), and the transform is a threshold, so a single sweep yields an adequate approximation and access caps in the reachable band. The differing action is concrete but modest - housekeeping that occasionally rescues in-flight work, which puts it just into the changes-a-real-decision band.

actionThatDiffers: You either start a second piece of work or walk away for a known interval, instead of babysitting the pane and re-checking it every 30 seconds to see whether the turn has landed.
why: No harness estimates turn duration and no shell loop can produce one: capture-pane tells you it is still emitting, never how much is left. So access is genuinely high, and because the number exists nowhere its value rests entirely on the estimator being accurate rather than on data being revealed. The differing action is concrete and recurs constantly (wait versus switch), but noisy ETAs blunt it, so impact lands in the upper changes-a-real-decision band rather than the loss-prevention band.
